notes.title: Hebel: breath, not conceit
notes.text: The Hebrew hebel (translated "vanity" in the KJV) literally means breath or vapor -- something that looks substantial for a moment and then is gone. It is the same word that opens Ecclesiastes ("vanity of vanities"). Modern English "vanity" suggests self-importance or conceit, which is not the sense here; the point is that even powerful people are as fleeting and insubstantial as a breath.
notes.source: Brown, Driver, Briggs, A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament (1906), s.v. hebel

notes.title: Chesed: covenant loyalty
notes.text: The Hebrew chesed, often rendered "mercy" in the KJV, is closer to covenant loyalty or unfailing love -- God's committed faithfulness to his promises, not simply leniency toward wrongdoing. Many modern translations render it "steadfast love" or "lovingkindness" for this reason. It is a different Hebrew word from the one usually translated "mercy" elsewhere (rachamim, compassion).
notes.source: Koehler & Baumgartner, The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, s.v. chesed

a bowing wall... a tottering fence
notes.title: A collapsing wall as a picture of a doomed attack
notes.text: City and terrace walls in the ancient Near East were built of mudbrick or unmortared stone and could fail suddenly after a leaning crack appeared -- a familiar, vivid image of something that looks standing but is already doomed. The psalmist pictures his attackers as already-collapsing, not as a real threat.
refs: Isaiah 30:13, which uses the same image
notes.source: Craigie, Psalms 1-50 (Word Biblical Commentary, 1983), on Psalm 62
